title: Ch-Y-H
hookLine: chai, chayim, life; chai adds to eighteen

cards: A check for eighteen dollars. Not twenty, not fifteen. Eighteen.
Or thirty-six, or a hundred and eighty. Open the cards at a bar mitzvah or a wedding and you may find these odd amounts, as if the guests shared a code. In a way they do.
Hebrew letters double as numbers, and the word for alive, chai, is spelled with just two of them: chet and yud. By the old count tradition uses, chet is eight and yud is ten. Eighteen.
So a gift of eighteen is a small wish folded into arithmetic, and the wish is life.

teach.h: CH-Y-H: ALIVE, A CREATURE, TO LIVE.
teach.b: Ch-Y-H. Chet, yud, heh. Turn it four ways.
First, the root itself. From these letters come chai, alive; chayah, a living creature; and the verb to live.

teach.h: CHAYIM: LIFE, WITH A PLURAL SOUND.
teach.b: Second, the word for life: chayim. It ends in the sound you hear on many Hebrew plurals, im. Some teachers like to read something into that, that a life is never just one thing.
That's a reading, not a grammar rule, but it sticks. Third, a verse where the root goes to work.
In Leviticus, God says of the laws, in the King James: "which if a man do, he shall live in them." The commandments are framed as something a person lives in, the way you live in a house.
Fourth, what the rabbis did with that one word.

teach.h: LIVE BY THEM, NOT DIE BY THEM.
teach.b: In the Talmud, tractate Yoma, the sage Shmuel reads it closely: live by them, and not die by them.
From this the rabbis teach that watching over a life, pikuach nefesh, pushes aside the rules of Shabbat.

Someone collapses on a Saturday afternoon: you drive, you call, you do what saves them, and the law itself tells you to. So the root that rides on a toast and hides in the number eighteen is also a rule with real weight.

how: Jews raise a glass with l'chaim, to life, at celebrations, and some give gifts and donations in multiples of eighteen, the number tradition reads from the letters of chai.

o: luck, a charm said to bring good fortune at parties
health, a toast wishing the body well and strong
alive, living; the root of chai and chayim

p: chet and yud, counted as numbers

s: the eighteen in gift amounts comes from the letters of chai
tradition counts chet as eight and yud as ten.
Jewish law says keep the Shabbat rules even when a life is at stake
the rabbis read "live in them" as live by them, not die by them: saving a life comes first.

games.q: it's Shabbat. a neighbor collapses and needs a hospital, and driving is normally off-limits today. what does Jewish law say?
o: drive, because saving a life comes first.
ask the neighbor to find someone else.
games.why: drive. Shmuel reads "he shall live in them" as live by them, not die by them: watching over a life sets the Shabbat rules aside.

practice: Bring to mind one person or place that keeps life going: a food bank, a clinic, a friend raising money, a neighbor who could use a meal.
Picture a gift for them in eighteens, eighteen dollars or cents or minutes or words of thanks; the size isn't the point, the number carries the wish.
Hold them in mind and say the word quietly, chai, and if you pray, you can ask a blessing on it.

wordCard.voice: Ch-Y-H. Chet, yud, heh: the root of chai, alive, and chayim, life. This week's roots ran stop, turn, pray, love, learn, awe, and now life. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: alive, living. chet and yud, from the root chet-yud-heh.

carryVoice: Your line: l'chaim, to life. The law, read this way, is for living. That's the week, with a glass raised.

sources.q: which if a man do, he shall live in them
